components.name: manual-source-review
components.description: This CBOM was produced by direct, manual inspection of protect_engine.py, unlock_engine.py, pdf_engine.py, and a project-wide grep for cryptography-related stdlib/third-party usage (hashlib, hmac, ssl, Crypto, cryptography, base64, md5/sha, rsa/aes/rc4, pbkdf, random.*, network modules). No automated CBOM-generation tool was run against this codebase -- none of the general-purpose CBOM scanners available to the author have first-class support for detecting PDF-library encryption usage (as opposed to direct calls to hashlib/cryptography/OpenSSL), so this is evidence-based manual extraction, not an automated-tool report. Confidence levels and exact source citations are given per finding below.

components.name: AES-256 (PDF Standard Security Handler)
components.description: VERIFIED (high confidence) from source: protect_engine.py defines `ENCRYPTION_METHOD = pymupdf.PDF_ENCRYPT_AES_256` (protect_engine.py, module-level constant, read from the installed pymupdf library's own enum rather than a hardcoded integer -- confirmed by the project's own test, tests/test_protect_engine.py line ~224: `assert protect_engine.ENCRYPTION_METHOD == pymupdf.PDF_ENCRYPT_AES_256`). protect_engine.protect_pdf() calls `doc.save(output_path, encryption=ENCRYPTION_METHOD, user_pw=user_password, owner_pw=owner_password, permissions=permissions, ...)` to ENCRYPT. unlock_engine.unlock_pdf() calls `doc.authenticate(password)` then re-saves with `encryption=pymupdf.PDF_ENCRYPT_NONE` to DECRYPT/strip protection. The project's own protect_engine.py docstring states this choice is deliberate: PyMuPDF also exposes PDF_ENCRYPT_RC4_40, PDF_ENCRYPT_RC4_128, and PDF_ENCRYPT_AES_128 but the code never uses them -- AES-256 is the only encryption method this application ever applies. UNVERIFIED FROM THIS REPOSITORY (medium/low confidence, spec-derived): the actual AES block-cipher mode, padding scheme, and key-derivation-from-password algorithm are implemented inside the MuPDF C library (bundled in the PyMuPDF wheel; see the companion SBOM's pkg:generic/mupdf component), not in any Python source file in this project, so they could not be confirmed by reading this codebase. The `mode`, `padding`, and `classicalSecurityLevel` fields below reflect what ISO 32000-2 / PDF 2.0 (and the Adobe Supplement for AESV3 under PDF 1.7) publicly specify for the PDF 'AESV3' / revision-6 standard security handler -- CBC mode with PKCS#7-style padding and a SHA-256-based key-derivation function -- cited as published-specification behavior, not independently verified against MuPDF's own C source (which is outside this repository).

properties.name: cbom:confidence:algorithmIdentity
properties.value: VERIFIED -- ENCRYPTION_METHOD = pymupdf.PDF_ENCRYPT_AES_256, protect_engine.py; call sites in protect_engine.protect_pdf() (encrypt) and unlock_engine.unlock_pdf() (decrypt/strip).

properties.name: cbom:confidence:modePaddingKdf
properties.value: UNVERIFIED FROM SOURCE -- derived from the public ISO 32000-2 PDF standard security handler specification for AESV3/R6, not from reading MuPDF's own C implementation (not present in this repository).

properties.name: cbom:unusedAlternatives
properties.value: pymupdf.PDF_ENCRYPT_RC4_40, PDF_ENCRYPT_RC4_128, and PDF_ENCRYPT_AES_128 are available in the pymupdf API surface but were confirmed, by full-project grep, to never be referenced anywhere in this codebase outside of explanatory comments in protect_engine.py listing them as options NOT chosen.

properties.name: cbom:keyLengthConstraint
properties.value: protect_engine.py: MAX_PASSWORD_LENGTH = 40 (both user and owner passwords are rejected above 40 characters before reaching pymupdf). This is a PDF standard security handler constraint on the password used for key derivation, verified directly from source.

properties.name: cbom:accessControlConfig
properties.value: protect_engine.py: DEFAULT_PERMISSIONS = 4095, built from pymupdf.PDF_PERM_PRINT | PDF_PERM_COPY | PDF_PERM_MODIFY (and other standard permission bits) -- the PDF permissions bitmask passed to doc.save(permissions=...). This is a standard-security-handler access-control configuration associated with the encrypted document (enforced by compliant PDF readers, not a cryptographic primitive itself), verified directly from source.

properties.name: cbom:defaultRejectEncrypted
properties.value: pdf_engine.validate_pdf(path, allow_encrypted=False) (the default used by every tool EXCEPT Unlock PDF) raises EncryptedPDFError whenever `doc.is_encrypted and doc.needs_pass` -- i.e. every other tool in the application refuses to open a password-protected PDF rather than attempting to bypass or guess its password. Verified directly from source, pdf_engine.py lines ~114-170.

properties.name: cbom:implementingLibrary
properties.value: pymupdf (Python binding) / MuPDF (bundled C library, Artifex Software) -- see sbom.cdx.json components pkg:pypi/pymupdf and pkg:generic/mupdf. This project's own Python source does not implement AES itself anywhere.

components.name: Python secrets module (CSPRNG) -- owner password generation
components.description: VERIFIED from source: protect_engine.py calls `owner_password = secrets.token_urlsafe(24)` to generate a random owner (permissions) password for every protect_pdf() call -- the end user never supplies or sees this value. Python's `secrets` module is documented (CPython standard library) to be suitable for managing secrets such as passwords and is backed by the OS's cryptographically secure random source (os.urandom(), e.g. getrandom()/BCryptGenRandom() depending on platform). The specific OS-level CSPRNG backing `os.urandom()` on any given deployment target was NOT independently verified here -- that is a property of the host operating system, not of this project's source.

properties.name: cbom:confidence
properties.value: VERIFIED -- exact call site: protect_engine.py, `owner_password = secrets.token_urlsafe(24)`.

properties.name: cbom:entropyBits
properties.value: 192 (24 random bytes, per the documented semantics of secrets.token_urlsafe(nbytes) in the Python standard library -- not independently re-derived from CPython's own source in this review, cited as documented stdlib behavior).

properties.name: cbom:lifecycle
properties.value: VERIFIED from source: the generated owner password is used once (passed into doc.save(owner_pw=...)), then explicitly deleted with `del owner_password` immediately after use, and is never logged, returned to the caller, written to disk, or displayed in the UI (verified: no reference to the owner_password variable after the del statement, and no logging call anywhere in protect_engine.py includes it).

components.name: PDF user (open) password
components.description: VERIFIED from source: a password string supplied via the application's UI (ui.py) is passed through protect_engine.protect_pdf() as `user_password` to `doc.save(..., user_pw=user_password, ...)`. This becomes the PDF 'open' password a reader must supply to view the document. The application performs only length validation (<=40 chars, matching MAX_PASSWORD_LENGTH) and a non-empty check before use -- no complexity/strength policy is enforced by this project's own code (any strength policy beyond that is whatever the user chooses). Not persisted by the application: no log statement, temp file, or output artifact in protect_engine.py/pdf_engine.py was found (by grep) to write this value anywhere other than the single doc.save() call.

relatedCryptoMaterialProperties.format: string (UTF-8, PDF standard security handler password, <= 40 characters enforced by this application)
